rv.q: It's hard to imagine six more exciting hours of vital, emotionally and intellectually engaging theater.
I can't remember being so ridiculously happy for the entirety of a Shakespeare performance since — let me think — August 2002.
It isn't so much that these astonishing actors are well-schooled in playing both comedy and tragedy, more that they see the tragic side of comedy and the comic side of tragedy.
And Shakespeare's language, as well as his meanings, have seldom been as clear.
So gallop, don't trot, to the Globe's repertory production of Twelfth Night and Richard III
Spacey's Richard is a master class in theatrical cunning, a performance that crackles with malevolent energy and dark humor that makes the villain's machinations utterly compelling.
They achieve a spectacle of surpassing elegance and buoyancy: We see a classic comedy and a bloody tragedy in their pure Shakespearean glory.
It's a fascinating choice, even if we lose a lot of Richard's evil edge.
Other warnings might have been issued.
There is a gaping hole where the charisma ought to be, and his seduction of Lady Anne, which is normally so creepily erotic, has hardly a spark of sex about it.

His imagination is so unbounded that anyone who relishes superlative acting can't take his or her eyes off him for fear of missing what unexpected subtle or broad gesture or inflection will occur next.
Same goes for this double-decker delight.
Plainly speaking, this Twelfth Night is a triumph.
That also leaves us to savor impeccable performances under Tim Carroll's direction.

Viewers of the Netflix political drama “House of Cards” might detect the influence of Richard III on Kevin Spacey’s Frank Underwood (Spacey appeared as an energetic Richard III at BAM last year): Richard’s ruthless scheming, shameless manipulation and direct asides to the audience as he confides to us his monstrous plans pretty much set the bar ...
But once ‘Richard’ takes a cue from its leading man and turns things down a notch, it finds its feet: a cool study in establishment evil.
Twelfth Night is, under Carroll's robust guidance, a joy — sly and bawdy and finally touching, without ever losing its glorious naughtiness.
